---
name: apple-hig
description: Use when designing, implementing, or reviewing interfaces for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, watchOS, CarPlay, or other Apple system experiences using Apple's Human Interface Guidelines. Routes to current platform, foundation, pattern, component, input, and technology guidance.
license: MIT
metadata:
  author: AyushRajSinghParihar
  source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines
---

# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support or product-feasibility decisions, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. For an exact component, technology, or unfamiliar term, search the
   [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md). It links directly to local
   topic procedures. Enter the procedure before its supporting reference. Do not
   load the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |
|---|---|
| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |
| Onboarding, loading, search, sharing, accounts, feedback, media, settings | [Patterns](subskills/apple-hig-patterns/SKILL.md) |
| Charts, images, text views, embedded web content | [Content](subskills/apple-hig-content/SKILL.md) |
| Lists, collections, split views, tab views, disclosure and grouping | [Layout and organization](subskills/apple-hig-layout-and-organization/SKILL.md) |
| Buttons, menus, toolbars, menu bar, ornaments and actions | [Menus and actions](subskills/apple-hig-menus-and-actions/SKILL.md) |
| Sidebars, tab bars, search fields, tokens and path controls | [Navigation and search](subskills/apple-hig-navigation-and-search/SKILL.md) |
| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |
| Touch, keyboard, pointer, focus, eyes, gestures, controllers and sensors | [Inputs](subskills/apple-hig-inputs/SKILL.md) |
| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

Platform: macOS. A routine successful save always triggers an alert. Irreversible archive deletion is titled Error with body Something happened; buttons are Yes and No. The harmless save alert defaults to Cancel. A second alert is presented over the first when sync fails. No screenshot or app execution is available.

# Apple HIG: Task scope, interruption and dismissal

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify whether the task needs inline content, a temporary presentation, an independent window or a scrolling container. Use Modality before choosing a blocking surface when interruption is in question.
2. Enter the specific Alerts, Sheets, Popovers, Panels, Windows or Action sheets procedure to resolve anchoring, size, urgency and platform-specific behavior.
3. Name every meaningful exit: commit, cancel, back, outside click, gesture, close or interruption. Preserve unfinished work and restore the parent selection/focus where appropriate.
4. Deliver a presentation/exit-state contract or an implementation correction. Verify all supported exits and data consequences instead of checking only that the surface appears.

## Enter the topic procedure

Read the selected topic’s SKILL.md before its supporting guidance. For a review,
inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make
the authorized change; for design or adaptation, produce a usable specification
or patch. Load related topics only when the chosen procedure calls for them.

- [Alerts](.topics/apple-hig-alerts/SKILL.md)

## Completion evidence

Report the concrete decisions or changes, their source support, and which checks
passed, failed or were not executed. A source citation or a list of links is not
the requested work product. Retain platform exceptions and unresolved source
conflicts; the absence of a platform subsection does not establish support.

name: apple-hig-alerts
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting critical alerts, consequential confirmations, button roles, defaults, and cancellation.

# Interrupt only for a decision that warrants it

Read [the alert guide](../../references/alerts.md). Apply the following as application advice and preserve the documented deliberate-destruction exception.

Inspect the triggering condition, urgency, reversibility, prior user intent, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Establish whether immediate attention is necessary. Do not turn every status update or startup network failure into an alert; ordinary undoable deletion can use recovery instead. Record evidence of the actual outcome and default-key behavior, not just button color.

Write a contextual neutral title and only useful supporting text; name outcomes instead of Yes/No. Use at most three buttons with meaningful roles and a safe Cancel beside destruction. Distinguish unexpected destructive consequences from confirmation of explicitly requested destruction: the latter may retain a normal default so Return confirms intent. Cancel is not the default; consider no default when deliberate reading is necessary. A single default completion acknowledgment should be Done, while OK can acknowledge purely informational content. Do not impose one platform's button geometry everywhere.

Implement the alert/handlers or deliver exact copy, role/default/order, trigger, and result specification; reviews must identify the specific misleading consequence or unnecessary interruption. Use fields only when resolution requires input and secure entry for passwords. Apply relevant platform accessory/cancellation rules: Mac suppression/Help only when useful, visionOS accessory limits and parent/space relationship, keyboard/remote alternate cancellation where supported. Post-action alternatives may belong in an action sheet.

**Worked transformation:** Before: an editor displays `Error 47` with OK/Cancel after an unrequested operation would overwrite unsaved work; Return commits overwrite. Decision: the consequence is unexpected and concealed. After: explain the conflicting draft, offer explicit safe recovery/cancellation and appropriately destructive replacement, and define a default that cannot accidentally accept unexplained loss.

Deliver the artifact and trigger/outcome/default contract. Verify Return, Cancel, supported escape, enlarged text, and repeated errors without stacked alerts. Fail for concealed loss, misleading action text, no safe cancellation, or routine status forcing interruption. Separate handler checks from native alert/assistive execution.

Use [action-sheets](../apple-hig-action-sheets/SKILL.md) for alternatives, [undo-and-redo](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-undo-and-redo/SKILL.md) for reversible work, or [modality](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-modality/SKILL.md) for surrounding exits.

# Apple HIG: End-to-end behavior and recovery

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Trace the person’s task from entry through completion, cancellation, interruption and recovery. Select the pattern procedure for the actual failure or desired behavior before selecting its controls.
2. Preserve the current work, selection and navigation context across the transitions that matter. Choose interruption or modality according to urgency and task scope, not visual emphasis.
3. For asynchronous or recurring work, separate current progress, eventual result, error recovery and unavailable capability. For audio/video/haptics, specify user control and environmental behavior.

name: apple-hig-modality
description: Use when choosing, reviewing, or adapting a modal task, its presentation, dismissal paths, nested flow, or protection of unfinished work.
---

# Resolve modality as a task contract

Read [the modality guide](../../references/modality.md). Use its platform facts as constraints; the decision process below is application advice. A large or fullscreen presentation does not by itself prove modality: establish whether the parent is blocked and what ends that mode.

## Inspect the interruption

Determine create, review, or adaptation mode from the request. Inspect the supplied flows, screens, implementation, or brief for the initiating action, parent context, reason to interrupt, task length, side navigation, and retained work. Identify the platform and whether the task must coexist with another document, window, or reference view. Record what is actually known: a screenshot cannot prove that the background is interactive or that dismissal discards data.

Describe the task in one outcome sentence and identify why normal navigation or an in-context control would be insufficient. If blocking the parent brings no clear decision/focus benefit, revise toward an in-context or nonmodal presentation. Do not preserve modality merely because the current mockup uses a dimmed background.

## Choose presentation and completion together

1. Separate urgent critical information, a scoped related task, an intentional choice, and substantial editing/immersion. Route urgent critical information to alerts, choices to action-sheets/confirmation-dialog guidance, and a short task attached to a parent to sheets or a suitable popover. A fullscreen editor can support substantial work without being modal; document blocking behavior explicitly.
2. Choose a platform-supported candidate and load that topic before prescribing its detailed interaction. A separate window can preserve parallel work on iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS. A popover must not be carried onto an unsupported platform or forced into a compact layout. A sheet's modality itself varies: iOS/iPadOS can support nonmodal sheets; Mac sheets block their parent while other app windows remain usable. For visionOS, distinguish a Shared Space presentation filling a window from Full Space immersion.
3. Keep a modal task narrow enough that the suspended parent remains understandable. If the flow has essential subviews, give it one understandable route and distinguish Back from exiting the task. If it becomes a miniature app with unrelated navigation, split work into ordinary navigation, a separate window, or another appropriate nonmodal workspace instead of adding layers of modal navigation.
4. Specify every available exit against the same data policy: explicit completion, Cancel/Close, interactive dismissal, platform keyboard/remote escape where supported, and any product-defined navigation away. For each exit state whether changes are committed, retained as a draft, discarded after a deliberate decision, or preserved while dismissal is cancelled. Protect created work regardless of whether the exit began with a gesture or a button. Ask about persistence only if the product contract cannot be inferred; otherwise state a reversible assumption and implement it consistently.
5. Name the task and exits so the person can predict the result. Provide a familiar visible exit, using the platform's placement conventions from the selected presentation topic. “Back” changes steps; it must not silently abandon the whole task. Keep relevant guidance close to the work rather than making a title carry instructions.
6. Resolve competing presentations. Dismiss one modal before presenting its replacement and retain only needed context. An alert may appear above modal content for a necessary decision; do not stack alerts. Define which view returns after the alert or replacement so a save/discard decision cannot strand the person or resurrect obsolete content.

Perform the requested action: implement the presentation/exit behavior in the supplied code, create a flow and state specification when designing, or produce a prioritized review grounded in identifiable transitions. Adaptation must revise the presentation and exit contract for the destination platform, not just rename a sheet.

## Deliver and verify

Provide the changed artifact plus a concise transition contract: entry → parent availability → task steps → completion → each dismissal path → resulting data and return destination. In a review, give the observed evidence, consequence, and concrete repair for each issue; list unseen behavior as an inspection question, not a defect.

Exercise or trace a clean exit and an exit after making an edit. Verify that button, gesture, and supported escape paths agree on data protection; Back preserves the task; completion updates the intended parent; reopening does not restore an obsolete transient view; and no second sheet or alert traps the flow. Inspect focus transfer and restoration in code and exercise them when a suitable runtime exists. Fail the design if there is no discoverable exit, unfinished work disappears through one route, a critical decision can be bypassed accidentally, or background blocking contradicts the task contract. Report native input, assistive technology, and Apple-device behavior as unverified when only static or Linux checks were possible.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A tablet archive app opens “Add Collection” as a sheet. Choosing a cover presents another sheet; a downward swipe from either screen loses the entered title. A top `Back` on the first screen dismisses everything.

**Decision:** Creating a collection is a narrow related task, but cover selection belongs within it. Dismissal and back-navigation need distinct contracts; every dismissal path must protect the edited title.

**After:** Keep one collection sheet with an internal cover-selection step. The first step has `Cancel` and `Done`; the cover step has `Back` returning with its choice. Specify a shared exit handler: clean dismissal closes; edited dismissal offers keep editing or the product's explicit save/discard resolution. Completion creates one collection and returns to the archive. Verify that the swipe and Cancel paths invoke the same protection and that Back never destroys the draft. This proposed flow is application advice, not an observation of an existing app.

## Conditional handoffs

Load sheets, alerts, popovers, action-sheets, panels, or windows only for the selected presentation's detailed rules. Use entering-data or undo-and-redo when persistence/recovery is the real problem; use accessibility when focus boundaries and exit discoverability need deeper treatment. Carry the transition contract into that work.

name: apple-hig-buttons
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting action buttons, including their labels, roles, emphasis, hit regions, and platform behavior.
---

# Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.
5. Only when the command has delayed completion, define the initiating, waiting, and resolved behavior. On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Specify how duplicate activation is handled and what success or failure means in the product; do not promise network completion from a press animation.

Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. For adaptation, map each affected control to its destination platform rather than copying appearance alone.

## Deliver and verify

Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. Fail the design if a destructive consequence is mislabeled, peer targets overlap, an icon has no discoverable name, or custom press feedback is absent. State separately which checks were inspected in source, exercised, or remain Apple-device checks; Linux inspection does not prove gaze, VoiceOver, haptics, or native rendering.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

**After:** Specify `Export…` as the prominent action opening export settings, `Remove Photos` as a lower-emphasis command with a visible Undo path, and `Done` for finishing metadata edits. Inspect actual save semantics before changing `Close` to `Done`. Verify the Return mapping, undo restoration, and that each accessible name matches the resulting action. These product choices are an example application, not facts about the unseen implementation.

## Conditional handoffs

Load alerts for consequential confirmation/default decisions; toggles or segmented-controls for persistent selection; pop-up-buttons or pull-down-buttons for menu-opening behavior; toolbars when placement belongs to window chrome; and accessibility when naming, focus, contrast, or target access needs deeper work. Keep this button contract as the input to the next topic.

# Alerts Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. An alert interrupts to communicate urgent, critical information and useful actions, including problems, unexpected data loss, or important confirmations. ## Best practices Reserve alerts for situations that warrant immediate attention. Put informational status in context when no action is required. Common undoable deletions generally need no confirmation; uncommon irreversible destruction does. Avoid startup alerts: cached or placeholder content with a discreet problem explanation is often a better response to an unavailable network. ## Anatomy Alerts are modal and adapt their appearance to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS rather than using one universal layout. ## Content Use a title, optional message, and up to three buttons. iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS can include text fields; macOS and visionOS can include an icon and accessory view. macOS additionally supports a suppression checkbox and Help button. Use direct, neutral, approachable wording without blaming the person or concealing severity. The title should explain what happened, its context, and cause as concisely as possible, generally within two lines. Avoid a bare error label or code. Complete-sentence titles use sentence case and punctuation; fragments use title case without punctuation. Additional text should add information in brief complete sentences. Clear action labels should make button explanations unnecessary; if instructions are unavoidable, use device-neutral language such as choose and the exact title without quotation marks. Include an input field only when resolving the situation requires it, with secure entry for passwords. ## Buttons Use short, usually one- or two-word, title-case action labels without punctuation. Prefer specific outcomes over Yes/No or ambiguous OK; reserve OK for purely informational acknowledgment. A cancellation action is always Cancel. Place the expected/default action at the trailing end of a row or top of a stack, with cancellation generally leading or at the bottom. Apply destructive styling to destructive consequences the person did not deliberately request. A confirmation of an explicitly chosen destruction, such as Empty Trash, can retain a normal default action so Return confirms intent. Always provide Cancel alongside destructive actions, but do not make Cancel the default. To force a deliberate reading, consider no default. A single default acknowledgment button should be Done rather than Cancel. Support familiar alternate cancellation where appropriate: Home Screen exit on iOS/iPadOS; Escape or Command-Period on attached keyboards in iOS/iPadOS/macOS/visionOS; Menu on the tvOS remote. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS or watchOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS Use action sheets for multiple choices following an intentional action. Keep titles and optional messages short to minimize scrolling, while accommodating enlarged accessibility text. ### macOS The app icon appears automatically but can be replaced. Repeating alerts can offer suppression; necessary details can use an accessory view, and Help can open documentation. Reserve a caution symbol for situations needing extra attention, particularly unexpected loss, rather than routine overwrite, save, or empty-trash tasks. ### visionOS In Shared Space, an alert sits slightly in front of its parent window and stays attached when the window moves. In Full Space, it centers in the wearer's field of view. An accessory view must be no taller than 154 pt and use a 16-pt corner radius. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Modality](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality) [Action sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets) [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: February 2, 2024, September 12, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Modality Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A modal mode blocks its parent until explicitly dismissed. It can deliver critical information, clarify a recent action, support a narrow task, or focus attention on an immersive/complex activity. Alerts are available across platforms, while activity views, sheets, and confirmation dialogs or action sheets provide context-specific options. For a distinct task, iOS, iPadOS, and macOS commonly use a sheet or popover; iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS can also use a separate window. Fullscreen experiences can also be nonmodal. ## Best practices Use modality only for a clear focus/decision benefit. Keep tasks brief and direct so the suspended context remains memorable. Avoid a miniature app inside the modal; if subviews are essential, offer one understandable route and distinguish back-navigation from dismissal. A fullscreen modal can suit substantial editing, camera, or media; in visionOS Shared Space it fills a window, while Full Space can create immersion. Provide an obvious familiar exit: often a top control or downward swipe on iOS/iPadOS/watch, or a body control on Mac/tvOS. Before losing created content through either gesture or button, explain consequences and offer appropriate save/discard choices. Identify the task with a clear title and necessary guidance. Dismiss one modal before showing another, keeping only the necessary context; an alert can appear over other modal content, but never stack multiple alerts. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, or watchOS. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) [Alerts](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts) [Popovers](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers) [Action sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets) [Activity views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/activity-views) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Style](#Style) - [Content](#Content) - [Role](#Role) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) A button performs an immediate action. Its visual style, visible symbol/text, and semantic role work together to explain what activation does. ## Best practices Allow enough surrounding space for clear separation and easy selection. General hit regions should be at least 44×44 pt; visionOS targets need 60×60 pt. Custom buttons always need press feedback. ## Style Prefer system styles for built-in states, accessibility, and appearance adaptation. Use one or two prominent buttons per view for likely actions. Distinguish a preferred option through style rather than making related buttons different sizes. Keep label colors distinct from colorful content; the default monochrome often works best over rich backgrounds. ## Content Use a familiar symbol for a familiar action; use a short title-case verb phrase when words are clearer. Mac and visionOS can provide brief hover tooltips; text-labeled buttons usually explain themselves. ## Role Normal has no special meaning; primary is the expected/default action; Cancel abandons the current action; destructive signals data loss. Roles affect rendering, such as accent fill for primary and red for destructive. Primary can respond to Return and close a temporary view. Generally assign primary only to a nondestructive likely action. Application advice: consult the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception before prescribing confirmation behavior. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS For delayed completion, show an activity indicator within the activating button, optionally changing its label to the current operation. The indicator replaces any button image while preserving context for the wait. ### macOS #### Push buttons The standard push button can show text, imagery, or both and can serve as default. Use flexible height for tall icons or multiple text lines, otherwise retain standard sizing. Append an ellipsis when the button opens another window/view/app for further input. Circle suits glyph-only content, rounded rectangle or capsule suits text, and capsule suits text plus glyph. Standard states supply feedback; custom hover effects are not supported. A look-triggered tooltip can explain a glyph. | Shape | Supported visual sizes | | --- | --- | | Circle | Mini 28 pt; small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt; extra large 64 pt | | Text capsule | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Text-and-icon capsule | Regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Rounded rectangle | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | Visual size does not remove the 60-pt targeting requirement. Reserve white fill with black content for the system's toggled state. Prefer round/capsule forms for steady gaze, and a capsule for a standalone button. Keep centers at least 60 pt apart; add 4 pt padding around buttons 60 pt or larger to prevent hover overlap. Avoid rows/stacks of mini/small buttons. Prefer rounded rectangles for vertical text stacks and capsules for horizontal rows. Standard sounds matter because visionOS provides no haptics. ### watchOS Inline buttons are capsules with a contrasting material. Put corner actions in a toolbar so the system relocates title/time and gives controls Liquid Glass. Full-width buttons suit primary actions. item.text: The brief verifies four issues: deletion copy hides the consequence, sync failure stacks alerts, routine saves interrupt the user, and the save alert defaults to Cancel. The deletion alert’s default is unknown; the guidance allows a normal default for explicitly requested destruction, so I won’t report that as a defect.

# Mac research archive: irreversible-delete alert audit

This is a specification review of "'`interface.md`, not an executed app audit. Rankings reflect potential consequence first, then interruption frequency. All four findings below are verified against the supplied description; implementation outcomes remain unverified.

## Ranked findings and decisions

| Rank | Verified evidence | Effect and correction | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 — High | Irreversible deletion is titled `Error`, says `Something happened`, and offers `Yes` / `No`. | Conceals the affected object, permanence, and action outcomes. Replace with a contextual deletion question, explicit irreversible consequence, and `Cancel` / `Delete Archive`. A deletion confirmation warrants interruption. The described buttons also lack the explicit Cancel label required alongside destruction; their actual handlers are unknown. | [Alerts: Best practices, Content, Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts#Content) |
| 2 — High | Sync failure presents a second alert over the first. | Competing modal decisions obscure the active task. Keep at most one alert; retain the deletion decision and record sync failure for in-context display, or present a necessary recovery alert only after the first closes and after revalidating relevance. | [Modality: Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality#Best-practices) |
| 3 — Medium | Every routine successful save triggers an alert. | Repeatedly blocks work without a consequential decision. Remove the alert; show a nonblocking `Saved` status in the archive context when useful. Do not infer sync success from local save success. | [Alerts: Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts#Best-practices) |
| 4 — Medium | The harmless save alert defaults to `Cancel`. | Cancel implies abandoning a task that already succeeded and is an inappropriate default. Removing this alert resolves the defect. If a separately justified completion acknowledgment is retained, use a single default `Done`; purely informational acknowledgment may use `OK`, with no invented cancellation effect. | [Alerts: Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts#Buttons), [Buttons: Role](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons#Role) |

These are source-backed findings. The exact copy, no-default choice, status treatment, and scheduling model below are product design decisions applying that guidance.

## Corrected behavior and control contract

Entry assumption: the person explicitly requests deletion of the selected archive. The brief does not establish the initiating command or deletion scope. Bind the confirmation to a stable archive identifier and display its actual name; verify the scope before shipping. Do not invent claims about attachments, backups, or deletion from other devices.

Proposed worked example, using the illustrative archive name “Field Notes”:

| | Before (supplied) | After (proposed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trigger | Irreversible archive deletion; initiating action unspecified | Person invokes deletion for Field Notes; no data changes yet |
| Title | `Error` | `Permanently delete “Field Notes”?` |
| Body | `Something happened` | `This will permanently delete this archive. You can’t undo this action.` |
| Actions | `Yes`, `No`; mappings/default unknown | Horizontal Mac row: `Cancel` leading, `Delete Archive` trailing |
| Default | Unknown | No default; unfocused Return does nothing |
| Cancel outcome | Unknown | Close confirmation; preserve archive, selection, and unfinished work |
| Delete outcome | Irreversible deletion described; handlers unseen | Explicit activation commits deletion of the confirmed archive only; update archive view after confirmed success |
| Concurrent sync error | Second alert above first | Record/coalesce error; no overlay alert; surface current sync status after dismissal |

`Cancel` has cancellation semantics. `Delete Archive` performs destruction, but for the assumed explicitly requested deletion it uses the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception: normal visual styling is permitted. Choose no default here to encourage reading the irreversible consequence; do not make Cancel the default. If the real flow exposes unexpected destruction instead, use destructive styling and explain that unexpected consequence. A normal Delete default allowing Return is permitted for deliberate destruction; it is not a verified violation in this interface. See [Alerts: Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts#Buttons).

Escape and Command-Period cancel the pending confirmation with the same data policy as Cancel. Focused-button activation remains available through the chosen toolkit’s ordinary keyboard interaction; no default does not mean disabling keyboard access. Do not bind bare Return globally to deletion. Restore focus to the initiating control after cancellation; after success, move to a meaningful remaining archive-list location. Focus behavior is a proposed contract requiring runtime verification.

Use Mac-appropriate standard button sizing and distinct, nonoverlapping targets; allow the archive name and translated labels to wrap or expand without hiding the permanent-loss message. Prefer system styles where available, but no Apple SDK is assumed. Do not add a caution symbol merely because this is a routine explicitly requested deletion. No suppression checkbox is proposed for this confirmation. See [Buttons: macOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons#macOS) and [Alerts: macOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts#macOS).

## Framework-agnostic transition specification

```text
state = idle | confirming(targetID, revision, returnContext) | deleting(targetID)
activeAlert = none | deleteConfirmation | recovery
pendingSyncIssue = none | latestRelevantIssue

on routineSaveSucceeded:
    update local save status to Saved without opening an alert
    leave sync status independent

on requestDelete(target):
    if state != idle or activeAlert != none: do not open another confirmation
    capture target ID, revision, display name, and return context
    state = confirming(...)
    activeAlert = deleteConfirmation
    block changes in the affected parent; do not globally block unrelated work
    render exact copy and buttons above, with no default action

on Cancel / Escape / Command-Period while confirming:
    dismiss confirmation; clear activeAlert; state = idle
    preserve data and restore return context
    reconcilePendingSyncIssue()

on explicitly activate Delete Archive while confirming:
    revalidate target identity, revision, and deletion eligibility
    if changed: close stale confirmation without deleting;
                explain changed target in context; require a fresh request
    otherwise:
        atomically leave confirming so repeated activation cannot submit again
        dismiss confirmation; clear activeAlert; state = deleting(targetID)
        perform deletion once; indicate pending work in context
        on success: update archive view; state = idle; restore meaningful focus
        on failure or uncertain result:
            reconcile actual archive state; never claim successful deletion
            state = idle; explain known failure and available recovery
        reconcilePendingSyncIssue()

on syncFailure(issue):
    pendingSyncIssue = coalesceByAffectedArchive(issue)
    if activeAlert == none and state == idle: reconcilePendingSyncIssue()

reconcilePendingSyncIssue():
    discard resolved or obsolete issues
    show relevant sync failure in context, with supported recovery actions
    if immediate user decision is genuinely necessary:
        wait until activeAlert == none and state == idle
        revalidate issue; then present one contextual recovery alert
    never stack alerts or replay duplicate stale errors
```

The scheduling and revalidation rules are proposed safeguards, not evidence of existing backend behavior. No retry or local-copy guarantee is promised without implementation evidence. A failed sync must not silently reinterpret the archive being confirmed. A later recovery alert must describe the actual problem and available actions rather than reuse `Error` / `Something happened`.

## Acceptance checks and results

**Passed — static audit only:** platform and irreversibility are explicit in the supplied brief; an irreversible-deletion confirmation is justified. The proposed specification names outcomes, provides safe cancellation, defines a no-default policy, and prevents stacked alerts on paper. These passes do not establish runtime compliance.

**Failed — supplied behavior:** consequential title/message clarity; specific action labels and explicit Cancel; routine-success interruption policy; save acknowledgment default; single-alert presentation policy. These failures come from the brief, not observed device execution.

**Not executed — implementation acceptance checks:**

1. Invoke deletion for a named archive: show the specified name and permanent-loss warning before mutation. Return with no focused button does not delete. Deliberately activate Delete Archive by keyboard and pointer: exactly one deletion request targets the confirmed ID.
2. Test Cancel, Escape, and Command-Period independently: no deletion, preserved work and selection, useful focus restoration. Test supported window-close/navigation paths: they must not bypass confirmation or commit deletion.
3. Change or remove the archive while confirmation is open: reject stale confirmation; never substitute another archive. Repeat activation during pending deletion: no duplicate request. Simulate success, failure, and uncertain completion: report only verified state.
4. Complete repeated routine saves: no alert or focus theft; Saved status reflects local success only. If a justified acknowledgment exists elsewhere, test its intended Done/OK behavior and default separately.
5. Trigger sync failure during confirmation, during deletion, and repeatedly: at most one alert; deletion choice remains understandable; errors are coalesced, revalidated, and surfaced without stale replay. Canceling deletion must not erase a relevant sync issue.
6. Render long names, enlarged text, and translated labels: no clipped consequence or overlapping controls. Verify actual focus order, button names, keyboard activation, and assistive announcement in the target implementation. Measure selectable regions from real layout/runtime evidence; no size defect is established by this brief.

## Evidence and limits

Only `interface.md` and installed local guidance were used. No screenshot, implementation, executable, Apple SDK, device, GUI, keyboard, or accessibility execution was available. Button geometry, actual roles/styles, delete default, Yes/No handlers, deletion scope, focus behavior, sync urgency, and persistence/recovery guarantees are unknown. No such unknown is ranked as an observed defect. The worked archive name is illustrative.

Instruction route read explicitly, with one file per shell command: installed `apple-hig/SKILL.md`; Presentation family → Alerts procedure → `presentation/references/alerts.md`; Patterns family → Modality procedure → `patterns/references/modality.md`; Menus and actions family → Buttons procedure → `menus-and-actions/references/buttons.md`. All paths were resolved within `.agents/skills/apple-hig/subskills/` for family material. Alerts owns confirmation/default/copy; Modality owns competing presentations/exits; Buttons covers each supplied Yes/No/Cancel control, including questions whose implementation is unseen.

The installed source guides identify a 2026-10-25 snapshot and are derived guidance, not SDK documentation or proof of independent source review. Official links above are attribution from those local guides; no web content was fetched. General button guidance prefers nondestructive defaults; the more specific alert guidance permits a normal default for deliberately requested destruction. This specification preserves that exception and selects the documented no-default option rather than asserting that deletion can never be default.
EOF'
